claims.text: Corrosion degradation versus protection retention in pre-exposure Q235 steel is controlled by the uniformity and integrity of its initially formed passive iron-oxide film.
A more homogeneous oxide layer inhibits aggressive high-temperature salt attack more effectively.
Fewer non-metallic inclusions or lower grain-boundary density produce a more homogeneous oxide layer.
Localized oxide-film defects accelerate corrosion through micro-galvanic effects.
As-received Q235 steel has inclusions and grain-boundary distributions capable of influencing corrosion behavior.
Mechanical polishing can modify the uniformity of the oxide film formed on Q235 steel.
Annealing can reduce relevant microstructural heterogeneities and thereby modify oxide-film uniformity in Q235 steel.
Exposure at 700–900 °C amplifies oxide-film formation dynamics and the effects of underlying microstructural heterogeneity.
Room-temperature corrosion of Q235 steel is less dependent on oxide-film integrity than high-temperature salt corrosion.
The relevant structural mediator is the density, adhesion, continuity, and defect distribution of the passive iron-oxide layer that forms spontaneously on Q235 steel.
Q235 steel forms an oxide layer during elevated-temperature aggressive-salt exposure.
The elevated-temperature oxide layer can act as a protective barrier against further corrosion.
Inclusions and regions of high grain-boundary density disrupt the oxide film and create weak sites for localized corrosion.
Relatively homogeneous regions maintain a coherent oxide film that retards further corrosive attack.
Polished or annealed samples will develop a more continuous and adherent oxide layer than untreated Q235 steel during high-temperature salt exposure.
Polished or annealed samples will exhibit lower mass loss than untreated samples during high-temperature salt exposure.
Polished or annealed samples will retain hardness better than untreated samples during high-temperature salt exposure.
Treatment-dependent differences in corrosion and mechanical degradation will be less pronounced at room temperature than at 700–900 °C.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to high-temperature salt exposure at 700–900 °C, while different corrosion mechanisms may predominate at room temperature.
